name: Rules Break
subtitle: Why hand-coded logic loses to learning

next.name: Learning From Data
next.tagline: The model never saw a rule. So what DID it learn from?

cards.objective: Create curiosity about how learning beats hand-coded rules
cards.hook: I bet you can't write 10 rules that beat a program that never saw a rule.
cards.statement: Hand-coded logic vs. something that learned from examples. Let's find out which one catches the sneaky stuff.

cards.objective: Define rules-based systems and why they crack
cards.hook: A rules-based system: if this, then that.
cards.statement: Classic spam filters are lists of suspects. Write a rule for every attack — and every new attack needs a new rule.
facts: A rule is a guess about the future, written in the past.
Every new attack ships a new rule — forever.

cards.objective: Let the learner run their own rule filter against an attack corpus
cards.hook: Your rules. Real attacks. Live score.
cards.statement: Turn rules on, run the attack, watch the leaks. Some attacks slip past no matter what — and one honest email might get caught anyway.

interaction.prompt: Toggle rules, then run the attack.

cards.objective: Force a commitment about rules vs learned patterns

interaction.prompt: Your rules caught 4 of 7 spam messages. A model that never saw a rule is about to face the same corpus. Who catches more?

options.label: My rules — the attacks match what I wrote
options.explanation: The next attack doesn't care what you wrote. Leet-speak, synonyms and new phrasings slip past every keyword you invented.

options.label: The model — it learned from examples, not keywords
options.explanation: The model never saw the word "free". It saw hundreds of spam examples and learned what spam looks like.

options.label: We tie
options.explanation: You caught the ones written to your rules. It caught the ones you never imagined. Not a tie.

cards.reveal: Rules memorize cases. A learned model generalizes a pattern. That gap only grows as attacks get sneakier.

cards.objective: Show the model beating the rule list on the same corpus
cards.hook: Now watch the model do it.
cards.statement: No rule was ever written for "fr33" or "100% win". The rules leak. The model doesn't — it learned the pattern, not the rule.

cards.objective: Compress the rules-vs-learning shift into one frame
cards.hook: Data → Model → Prediction. That's the whole shift.
cards.statement: Rules are written for cases you can imagine. Models learn patterns you can't.
facts: A rule says "if this, then that".
A learned model says "based on what I've seen, this looks like that".
The model's "rules" come from examples, not engineers.

cards.objective: Check that the learner can name why the model won

interaction.prompt: Why did the model catch messages your rules missed?

options.label: It's smarter than your rules
options.explanation: It's not smarter — it never "knew" anything at all. It learned.

options.label: It generalized a pattern from examples
options.explanation: Hundreds of spam examples taught it what spam looks like — including phrasings no one wrote down.

options.label: Someone hid extra rules inside it
options.explanation: That's the trick — nobody can hide rules it never saw. The pattern came from data.

cards.reveal: Generalization: catching things you never explicitly listed.

cards.objective: Close the module by showing why rules do not scale
cards.hook: One new attack. One new rule. Forever.
cards.statement: A model doesn't append rules — it updates its understanding. And the next wave of spam writes itself into next week's examples.
facts: Every rule is debt someone maintains.
Every model is a one-time understanding that keeps improving.
The spam adapts. So must we.
